name: Rat-Catcher
text: Between two torches sits a wiry woman with her leg in a splint and a ratting pole across her knees, and beside her stand a dozen stoppered jars of green bile, drawn up like soldiers. "The bone came through the skin and I set it myself," she says, "but the bleeding will not stop." She lifts her chin toward the jars. "That's fever cure for Saint Agatha's. There are forty children up there who think that nothing can kill me, and my daughter thinks the same, but they are mistaken."

options.label: Give her a healing potion
options.outcome: She drinks, and the grey goes out of her lips. "My girl is called Lena," she says, as she takes up her jars again to label them. "If ever she finds you she will want to pay you back, and you must let her, for she's a stubborn one."

thread.hint: Somewhere above, a girl is listening for her mother's limp on the stairs.

options.chronicle: Stopped Marta the rat-catcher bleeding out. She made sure of my name.

road.hint: A daughter may come down one day to repay her mother's healing.

options.label: Pack the wound and reset the splint yourself

pass.outcome: You pack the wound, bind it off above and set her splint straight, and the bleeding slackens to a seep. "Wherever did you learn that?" she asks you in wonder.

thread.hint: Somewhere above, a girl is listening for her mother's limp on the stairs.

pass.chronicle: Packed and bound Marta the rat-catcher's leg. She was grateful.

fail.outcome: The cloth soaks through as fast as you can pack it, and Marta grows quiet as she watches your hands. "Go on, now," she says at last, "and tell Lena that her mam got the bile."
fail.chronicle: Botched Marta the rat-catcher's wound. Never learned if her leg held.

road.hint: A wound may be bound with skill and no potion.

options.label: Keep your supplies and tell her to hold pressure
options.outcome: "Maybe someone else will come," she says, and leans upon the wound with both hands, though you both know how small that hope is.
options.chronicle: Left a rat-catcher holding her own wound shut.

road.hint: A bleeding woman may not last until some other helper passes by.

options.label: Take the jars and her potions
options.outcome: "Those are for sick children," she says. She cannot stand, and so she does not try. "My daughter's name is Lena, if ever you should grow a conscience and want someone to ask pardon of."
options.chronicle: Robbed a rat-catcher's satchel. It was children's medicine.

road.hint: Medicine meant for sick children is a heavy thing to steal.

name: Lost Girl
text: A little girl of about seven sits against the wall hugging her knees, with a stub of candle beside her. When she sees the silver pendant at your belt she stiffens from head to foot. "That's Mama's," she says. "She gave it me to hold till she got back, and I dropped it when the rats came." She works a small silver ring from her finger and holds it out to you in a shaking hand. "You can have this instead. It's real silver. Please let me have hers."

options.label: Give her the pendant and tell her to keep her ring
options.outcome: She looks from the ring to you, as though you had broken some law that no one ever told her of. Then with both hands she draws the pendant over her head, and the candle trembles no longer. She gets up and goes toward the stairs, holding the pendant out before her like a lantern.
options.chronicle: Gave a little girl her mother's pendant. Refused her ring for it.

road.hint: A frightened child will offer all she has, and she need not be made to pay it.

options.label: Give her the pendant and take the ring
options.outcome: She presses the ring fiercely into your palm, as if a bargain could make all things safe. "Now it's fair," she says, and she clutches the pendant to her and runs away toward the stairs.
options.chronicle: Traded a girl of seven her mother's pendant for her silver ring.

road.hint: A little girl may feel the safer for paying with her ring.

options.label: Ask where her mama went
options.outcome: "She went down for Benno's medicine, because he's got the fever. She said seven sleeps." The child counts upon her fingers until she runs out of fingers. "It's been more than all of them."

options.label: Keep the pendant. You need every edge down here
options.outcome: She neither argues nor weeps, but watches you put it away as children watch a thing that they will remember when they are grown. After a little while she gets up and goes toward the stairs without it.
options.chronicle: Kept a pendant a little girl said was her mother's.

road.hint: A child's mother may know her pendant again, if she should see it.

name: Grumwald
text: A bridge of rope hangs over a black gulf, and at its near end a troll as great as a hay cart sleeps sitting up, with his chin on his breast and one eye not wholly shut, snoring like a millrace. Beside him are a box with a slot in it and a board lettered with great care: TOLL A COIN. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY. The box is half full, and it seems that no one would ever know what you did here.

options.label: Drop a coin in the box
options.outcome: At the clink of the coin one yellow eye opens, rests upon you and closes again. "Forty years I've sat here," the troll rumbles out of his sleep, "and you're the ninth today." The bridge does not so much as creak as you pass over it.
options.chronicle: Paid a sleeping troll's toll. The ninth that day, he says.

road.hint: An honest traveller will pay the toll though the keeper is asleep.

options.label: Cross quietly
options.outcome: You cross upon your toes, and the bridge bears you as surely as it would have borne one who paid, while behind you the snoring goes on unchanged.
options.chronicle: Crossed a sleeping troll's bridge without paying.

road.hint: The troll's bridge will bear you whether you have paid the toll or no.

options.label: Empty the box
options.outcome: You lift out the coins in two fistfuls, and the troll sleeps on. He had trusted his box to the honesty of all who pass, and it seems that none will ever know what became of it.
options.chronicle: Emptied a sleeping troll's honesty box, forty years' tolls. Unseen.

road.hint: An unguarded box may be a trial of honesty.

name: Pomfrey Quill
text: Upon a trunk sits a small round man in an absurdly fine coat, his moustache immaculate and his face full of terror. "Pomfrey Quill, alderman and collector," he says. "I followed the adventurers down from the town, for I thought there would be profit in it." He pats the trunk. "I have rings here, a cloak that shimmers and a holy bell from Kildare, the fruit of ten years' collecting. Walk me to the up-stair and you may have your pick." You notice that the tongue of the bell is tied with a strip of a nun's grey veil, so that it cannot ring.

on_arrive.outcome: At the stair Quill throws open the trunk. "Take your pick as we agreed, saving only the bell," he says, and he climbs away with the bell in both arms and never looks behind him.
on_arrive.chronicle: Saw Alderman Quill out, had my pick. Kept quiet on whose bell it is.

on_fail.chronicle: Lost Alderman Quill on the stairs. He would not leave his trunk.

options.label: Walk him to the stair for your pick of the trunk
options.outcome: "Splendid, oh, splendid! You shall go first, and I shall carry, er, the trunk."

road.hint: A reward out of a collector's trunk may be someone's stolen treasure.

options.label: Tell him whose bell that is

pass.outcome: "That is Brigid's bell," you tell him, "from Kildare, which is Cill Dara, the church of the oak. Her nuns tended a fire there in her honour, nineteen of them, each for a night in turn, and on the twentieth night they left it in her own care." Quill grows pale beneath his moustache. With fussy fingers he picks the veil loose from the tongue, and the bell rings once of itself, as clear as a morning. "You must have your pick, then, for the lesson," he says, but you will take nothing. He wraps the bell in his own scarf and stumps away toward the up-stair, and he seems strangely lighter.
pass.chronicle: Told Quill whose bell he had, took no reward. It rang when untied.

fail.outcome: You guess at a saint and name the wrong one. Quill sniffs and says, "Provenance, my dear, is whatever the buyer believes," and so the tongue of the bell stays tied.
fail.chronicle: Named the wrong saint for Quill's bell. He kept it, tongue still tied.

road.hint: A collector might untie the bell, if he were told whose it is.

options.label: Give him food and point him to the stair
options.outcome: He clutches the food to his chest. "I'll give you a tip for nothing," he says. "I had a buyer once who wanted four things that don't belong together. A man who held all four, he said, need never fear the one collector whom nobody outbids. I told him that I sell rings." With that he hoists his trunk and shuffles away.
options.chronicle: Fed and sent up Alderman Quill. He spoke of a collector nobody outbids.

road.hint: A collector, once fed, may speak of the last collector of all.

options.label: The trunk stays, as your toll
options.outcome: "But that's everything I have," he begins, and then he sees your face and lets go of the trunk. All that he gathered in ten years of collecting goes into your pack with room to spare.
options.chronicle: Robbed an alderman's trunk, mostly stolen goods already.

road.hint: Goods that were stolen once are none the cleaner for a second theft.

name: Burdened Knight
text: In the corridor a knight kneels, bowed double beneath a black stone lashed to his pack, and in his hands he cradles a crystal vial that shimmers. "My wife Elspeth is dying, and this cordial is her only hope," he says, "but the stone is cursed. I cannot put it down, and it grows heavier with every step." He lifts his reddened eyes to you. "If another takes it up willingly the curse will go with it, and at an altar it may be broken. I know what it is that I ask."

options.label: Take the lodestone so he can reach his wife

oath.what: Carry his lodestone to an altar, where it can break.

options.outcome: The stone settles into your pack like a dead thing. Sir Aldric rises weeping and runs for the stairs with never a look behind him, and from this hour both the burden and the promise are yours.

thread.hint: Somewhere above, a woman is lighting a candle for a knight.

options.chronicle: Took Sir Aldric's lodestone so he could climb home to his wife. Heavy.

road.hint: A burden taken up for a knight may be laid down in more ways than one.

options.label: Ask him how the stone came to him
options.outcome: "There was a horse thief whom I was to bring to the assize, and I hanged him from an oak to save a day's ride." He swallows. "A week afterward his brother found the horse where it had strayed, grazing in a ditch, and when I went back to look, the stone lay upon the grave."

options.label: Tell him you cannot carry it
options.outcome: "I know," he says. "God forgive me, I know it." He does not rise from his knees, and long after you have turned the corner you can hear the stone grinding against his armour.
options.chronicle: Left a knight kneeling under his stone.

road.hint: A knight must kneel beneath his stone until another will lift it.

options.label: Take the cordial for yourself
options.outcome: "I am sorry, Sir Knight," you say. He stares at you, for he knows there was another way and has seen you choose against it, and as you drink, warmth floods through all your body.
options.chronicle: Drank a dying woman's cordial before her husband's eyes.

road.hint: The cordial would heal you, though it was meant for a dying wife.

name: Young Thief
text: A boy stands at bay in a blind alley with a bag of coins clutched to his chest and one eye swollen shut, and between you and him stands Hanne, a broad woman with flour to her elbows and a rolling pin. "If I lose the shop, nobody on Tallow Lane eats bread this winter," she says. "Rosie's only eight," says the boy, whose name is Tam, "and she doesn't know what rent is." They both turn to you as though you were the magistrate, and all the while Tam's good eye keeps straying to your purse.

options.label: Make Tam give the coins back
options.outcome: Tam hands over the bag without a word. Hanne counts it twice, and then she breaks a heel from the loaf in her apron and gives it to him, though she will not look at him. "That's no payment," she says. "That's for Rosie."
options.chronicle: Made Tam give back a baker's till. She gave him bread anyway.

road.hint: Stolen is stolen, but a hungry boy can work.

options.label: Let Tam keep them. Rosie is eight
options.outcome: Tam runs, and this time Hanne does not give chase. She sits down on the steps with the rolling pin across her knees. "Three alleys get their bread from me," she says wearily, to no one at all.
options.chronicle: Let a boy keep a baker's rent for his sister. Three alleys go hungry.

road.hint: A widow's oven feeds three alleys.

options.label: Pay Hanne back from your own purse
options.warning: Tam's good eye keeps straying to your purse.
options.outcome: Hanne takes your coins with the look of one who has been handed what she never asked for. While you are counting into her apron Tam is counting out of your purse, and he is gone before you feel it, so that all anyone has learned by your kindness is where you keep your money.
options.chronicle: Paid a young thief's debt. He robbed my purse while I counted.

road.hint: Gold may pay a young thief's debt and teach him nothing.

options.label: Set Tam to work the debt off at Hanne's oven

pass.outcome: You lay out the bargain: Tam shall haul flour before dawn, Hanne shall take a copper a sack off what he owes the till, and meanwhile Rosie shall eat from the shelf of day-old bread. Hanne considers the boy's thin arms. "He'll do," she says. "He's quick, I'll give him that."

delayed.text: Upon a ledge a bundle of cloth is waiting for you, still warm, and someone has drawn a loaf upon it in flour.
delayed.chronicle: Hanne's bread found me further down. Tam must still be hauling flour.

pass.chronicle: Talked a baker into hiring the boy who robbed her.

fail.outcome: Hanne will have no thief at her oven, and you cannot find the words to move her. Tam bolts past you both, and the coins go with him and are never seen by you again.
fail.chronicle: Failed to make peace between Hanne and Tam. He ran with the coins.

road.hint: A young thief might work off his debt at the baker's oven.

name: Injured Cartographer
text: In a nest of careful maps sits a young woman in cracked spectacles, with her left arm hanging crookedly and one side of her face turned purple. She is trying to ink a corridor with her right hand instead, and the line wavers. "Twelve years I have made maps," she says, not lifting her eyes, "and never before have I drawn a bad line. I must have something for the pain or I cannot hold the pen, and the pen is all that I have."

options.label: Give her a healing potion
options.outcome: She flexes her drawing hand with a gasp and caps the vial. "I shall write your name upon the map, just here," she says, "and I will tell you one thing for nothing. There is a floor below that I cannot draw, for its walls will not hold still for the pen. The old Greeks never trusted a map in such a place, but put their trust in string."

delayed.text: On the stair a rolled map waits for you, tied with green ribbon, and written in its corner in a very steady hand are these words: A good person stood here.
delayed.chronicle: Found Helena's map of this floor, with my name in the corner.

options.chronicle: Gave Helena the mapmaker my potion. She will put me on a map.

road.hint: A mapmaker who is healed may send a true map after you down the road.

options.label: Set the bone yourself

pass.outcome: You brace her elbow and pull. She screams once, magnificently, and when it is over the arm is straight and bound to a ruler. "Barbarian," she says, and bends to her drawing again.

delayed.text: On the stair a rolled map waits for you, tied with green ribbon, and written in its corner in a very steady hand are these words: A good person stood here.
delayed.chronicle: Found Helena's map of this floor, with my name in the corner.

pass.chronicle: Splinted Helena the mapmaker's arm with a ruler. She drew me a map.

fail.outcome: You pull at the wrong angle and feel the bone grate, and Helena turns white and falls senseless across her maps. When she comes to herself she waves you away with her good hand. "Go," she says. "I shall learn to draw with the wrong hand."
fail.chronicle: Botched setting Helena's arm. She must learn to draw wrong-handed.

road.hint: Careful hands might set a mapmaker's broken arm.

options.label: Tell her you cannot spare it
options.outcome: She nods. "Go, then. I have lived through worse," she says, and with clenched teeth she grips the pen in her right fist and goes on drawing her wavering line.
options.chronicle: Left Helena the mapmaker hurt, drawing with the wrong hand.

road.hint: An injured mapmaker will stay at her work, whether helped or no.

options.label: Take her maps. They're worth a fortune
options.outcome: "That is my life's work, twelve years of it!" She snatches at the maps with her one good arm, but it is not enough, and rolled among them you find a scroll in no hand of hers.
options.chronicle: Robbed Helena of twelve years of maps. They sold well.

road.hint: The labour of twelve years might be carried off in a moment.

name: Old Warrior
text: An ancient warrior sits sharpening a broken sword, and the whetstone slips again and again from his fingers. Beyond the corner something great growls, and something else gives answer. "They will come in ten minutes," he says. "I have held this corridor three days, with eleven farmers behind me, and two of them babies. They are from Glimmerdeep, a farm in the caves off the upper stair, and the ghouls found it." He tests the broken blade. "It broke on the last of those that came, and without a weapon the reckoning goes against me." You see that the scratch upon his sword arm has turned black as far as the elbow.

options.label: Give him a weapon from your pack
options.warning: You see that the scratch upon his sword arm has turned black as far as the elbow.
options.outcome: He takes it, tries the weight and nods. "This will serve," he says. Before you reach the next corridor you hear the first clash behind you, and sooner than you could wish you hear it cease, and you know that he has fallen. One by one the lanterns of the farmers scatter into the side passages.
options.chronicle: Gave Konstantin my spare blade to hold a corridor. Fear most farmers died.

road.hint: Before you arm an old warrior, look well at his wounded arm.

options.label: Count the enemy with him

pass.outcome: You reckon it aloud, six ghouls and a troll against one good arm, and he hears the answer. "Then I hold the door, and you take them out by the side," he says, and does not argue, for he has been waiting to hear another say it. You lead the eleven farmers out through the drainage cut with the babies on their hips, and for a long while you can hear the broken sword ringing behind you.
pass.chronicle: Konstantin held the door. Took his farmers out the back.

fail.outcome: Your reckoning is wrong, for there are more than you thought, and they come early. In the confusion you bring four of the farmers out, and Konstantin dies behind you.
fail.chronicle: Miscounted the foe. Four of eleven farmers got out. Konstantin died.

road.hint: When a door cannot be held, seek another way out.

options.label: Stand and fight beside him
options.outcome: Back to back you hold the way until the torches burn low, and the farmers live. When it is over Konstantin sits down and does not rise, for the black has reached his heart. "It was a good fight," he says, "and better company."
options.chronicle: Held a corridor with Konstantin. The farmers live. He died after.

road.hint: A doomed warrior need not make his last stand alone.

options.label: Wish him luck and walk on
options.outcome: "There are no hard feelings," he says, and turns to face the corridor with the broken sword. "A broken sword slew a dragon once, after a smith had taken a second turn at it."
options.chronicle: Left Konstantin with half a sword. His saga: one reforged slew a dragon.

road.hint: A broken sword, forged anew, was once the bane of a dragon.

name: Grain Committee
stance_note: Steel-man: Varsk is right that the city is starving, and he is not a sadist. The lean (the calculation problem; the requisition record) is carried by the pass text, not by a lecture.

authority.who: Commissar Varsk and the Grain Committee
authority.why: Takes a village's seed by list and pays informers.

text: Off the Labyrinth's upper stair lies a little hamlet under the earth, with barley beneath a sun-stone, beds of mushrooms, and a cart half laden with sacks. A thin man in a grey coat, a commissar of the city, reads from a list while two soldiers bear seed out of a cellar. A woman holds one sack to her breast. "That is next spring," she says. The commissar does not raise his voice as he answers her. "Every sack in a farmer's cellar is a child in the city who does not eat. I am not a cruel man, but I can count." Behind the cellar door you see that one sack lies forgotten.

options.label: Hide the forgotten sack in your pack
options.outcome: The soldier who searches you is himself a farmer's son. He feels the sack at the bottom of your pack, looks you full in the eye, and writes down a fine instead. When the cart is gone the woman takes back the sack in silence, and she has put it into the ground before the torches are changed.

delayed.text: At the foot of the stair someone has left a sack tied with village string, and in it are barley bread, onions, and a child's drawing of you.
delayed.chronicle: Thwaite left me food and a drawing of me. Kept the drawing.

options.chronicle: Hid Thwaite's seed sack from the Committee. A farm-boy soldier let it go.

road.hint: If one sack of seed were hidden, a village might have bread next year.

options.label: Tell the commissar where the sack is
options.outcome: The commissar Varsk thanks you formally, pays you from a strongbox and writes your name in a different list. The woman watches the last sack go up the stair and says nothing, for there is nothing left to her now that she could plead for.
options.chronicle: Sold out a village's last seed sack. The commissar wrote my name down.

road.hint: An informer's name is written down in a list too.

options.label: Ask him who will decide next spring's needs

pass.outcome: You ask how many sacks the city will need next spring, and he names a number. You ask how he knows it, and he names another. Then you ask who is to plant when there is no seed, and what the city will eat in the spring that follows. By now his soldiers are listening. One of them comes from a village, and he sets down his sack, and after him the other does the same. Varsk writes for a long while, and when he departs his cart is but half full.

delayed.text: At the foot of the stair someone has left a sack tied with village string, and in it are barley bread, onions, and a child's drawing of you.
delayed.chronicle: Thwaite left me food and a drawing of me. Kept the drawing.

pass.chronicle: Asked the commissar about next spring. No answer. His soldiers took note.

fail.outcome: He has an answer out of his list for every question, and though there is a flaw in it you cannot put it into words, so that the cart goes away full.
fail.chronicle: Lost the argument with the commissar. The grain cart left full.

road.hint: Even a man with a list cannot know what a village will need next spring.

options.label: Walk on. It's not your village
options.outcome: The cart creaks away up the stair, and behind you the woman still holds her one sack, which the soldiers have not yet noticed.
options.chronicle: Walked past a village's grain being seized. Not my quarrel.

road.hint: When seed is carted away, hunger may follow in the spring.

name: Grieving Father
text: On a fallen pillar sits an old soldier, holding a child's blanket faded almost to white. At the sight of the sword you carry he stands so quickly that his knees crack. "That is my boy's," he says. "See, there is his name on the crossguard, CORIN. He came down six months ago to prove himself." His hands tremble. "Did you find him? Was there a body?" There was none, and the sword is the finest blade that you have ever owned.

options.label: Give him his son's sword
options.outcome: Marcus holds the sword to his breast and shuts his eyes. "He was a good boy," he says. "He was such a good boy." Then he walks toward the stairs, bearing sword and blanket, and he does not look behind him.
options.chronicle: Gave Marcus Hale his son's sword, the best blade I had.

road.hint: The finest blade you carry may rightly belong to a grieving father.

options.label: Tell him it was found point first
options.outcome: "It was found point first in the ribs of a wyrm," you tell him. "Whatever slew him, he hurt it sorely." Marcus lets out a long breath, as though he had held it for six months. "Point first," he says. "That's my boy."

options.label: "I need it to get down alive. If I live, I'll bring it home to you."
options.outcome: Marcus looks long upon the sword and afterward upon you. "That is what he would have said," he answers. "Bring it back in your own hand, then, and do not be carried home beneath it." He tells you the way to his house, and then tells it again lest you forget.
options.chronicle: Owe Marcus Hale his son's sword, if I live. Have the way to his house.

road.hint: A father might lend the sword, if he were told truly of your need.

options.label: Tell him you found no such blade
options.outcome: Marcus looks at the sword and reads the name CORIN upon the crossguard, so that he knows full well you are lying. He sits down again without a word and bows his head over the blanket in his lap.
options.chronicle: Lied to Marcus Hale about his son's sword. The name is on the crossguard.

road.hint: No lie can hide a name cut upon a crossguard.

name: Last Potion
text: Against the wall two soldiers lie in much blood: Dafydd, who is nineteen, with both hands pressed to the wound in his belly, and Sergeant Ilse, grey at the temples, with a gnoll's spear-head still in her thigh. If you carry healing, there is enough for one of them. "Give it to the boy," says Ilse. "I've had my years." "Don't you dare," says Dafydd. "She carried me, so don't you dare."

options.label: Heal Dafydd
options.outcome: The wound closes beneath his hands, and Ilse smiles to see it. "Good lad," she says. "Now go and be worth it." She is dead before he has finished rising to his feet.
options.chronicle: Gave Dafydd my potion on Sergeant Ilse's order. She died.

road.hint: A sergeant may give her last order to save a younger soldier.

options.label: Heal Ilse
options.outcome: Ilse comes up swearing at you, at him and at all gnolls, but Dafydd does not wait for the argument. When she turns to him he lies dead already, and he is smiling as though he had won some victory.
options.chronicle: Healed Sergeant Ilse against her orders. Dafydd died.

road.hint: A young soldier may be willing to die that his sergeant may live.

options.label: Split the dose carefully between them

pass.outcome: Half goes to the belly, which you pack and bind, and half to the thigh when you have drawn the spear-head. It should not suffice, and yet it does, though barely, and the two rise up together, holding to each other like drunkards.
pass.chronicle: Split one potion between Ilse and Dafydd. Both live.

fail.outcome: You divide it into two half measures for two whole wounds, and then you can only sit beside them while it fails and they die.
fail.chronicle: Split the dose wrong. Ilse and Dafydd both died.

road.hint: With skill and care, one draught might be made to serve two wounds.

options.label: Keep what you carry and sit with them
options.outcome: Ilse tells Dafydd of her farm and of her husband's terrible cheese, and he is still laughing at the cheese when death comes softly for them both.
options.chronicle: Kept my potion and sat with Ilse and Dafydd as they died.

road.hint: A draught saved for a later day will not help two who are dying now.

name: Two Prisoners
text: Two men in torn black cassocks hang from manacles a yard apart, each tonsured as a priest and each scored all over with ritual cuts. "He is the cultist, and he is wearing my robe," cries the man on the left. "Free me, for the love of God!" "He took my name with all the rest," says the man on the right. "Ask him anything." The manacles hum, and the magic of a scroll would surely overload them. Cultists in these halls have been known to wear a captured priest's robe.

options.label: Question them both on the Pater Noster

pass.outcome: The man on the left stumbles at "forgive us our trespasses", and he knows it. The man on the right gently finishes the prayer for him. "He has been practising," he says then, "but not for long enough." And so you break the chains of the right-hand man.
pass.chronicle: Two men claimed one priest's robe. Freed the one who knew the Our Father.

fail.outcome: Both of them pray as men who have prayed all their lives. You cannot tell. Since there is no one to fetch who might judge between them, you leave them in their chains.
fail.chronicle: Could not tell priest from cultist. Left both in chains.

road.hint: The true priest should know his prayer from end to end.

options.label: Free whichever one is begging hardest
options.warning: Cultists in these halls have been known to wear a captured priest's robe.
options.outcome: You break the chains on the left. The man drops and stands, and for a moment he regards you with true gratitude. Then he smiles upon the other prisoner and walks away whistling, and the man on the right closes his eyes and begins to pray for you.
options.chronicle: Freed the louder prisoner. He left whistling. The other prayed for me.

road.hint: The prisoner who begs the loudest may have borrowed his robe.

options.label: Use one scroll on both chains at once
options.outcome: The binding flashes and both sets of manacles fall. The true priest, Father Anselm, drops to his knees, but Morrow the cultist lands upon his feet and is gone before the other has finished thanking God. Anselm gazes after him. "You will see him again," he says, "and I am sorry for it."
options.chronicle: Freed both. Morrow the cultist ran. Father Anselm says I will meet him again.

road.hint: If both prisoners go free, you may meet the guilty one again.

options.label: Leave them both
options.outcome: Two voices follow you down the corridor, one cursing and the other praying, until at last you cannot tell the one from the other.
options.chronicle: Left two men in chains, one cursing me and one praying.

road.hint: A cassock cannot show which of two men is the true priest.

name: Dying Knight
text: A knight sits with his breastplate split and a mortal wound beneath it, in the careful dignity of one who knows how he will spend his last minutes. A fine sword lies across his knees and his dented shield beside him. "My daughter Annalise drew me a picture before I left," he says. "I took it for a horse, but she said it was a dragon." He comes near to laughing. "My squire Tobyn went on ahead, and he will think that I left him. If you have a potion, I do not ask it to save me, but only for the pain."

options.label: Give him a healing potion for the pain
options.outcome: He drinks, and the pain goes out of his face. From within his breastplate he unfolds a child's drawing, and he gazes long upon it. "It is a beautiful dragon, Annalise," he says.
options.chronicle: Gave dying Ser Brennan my potion for the pain.

road.hint: A potion that cannot save a dying knight may still ease his pain.

options.label: Swear to give his sword to Tobyn

oath.what: Give his sword to his squire Tobyn and tell him he was not left behind.

options.outcome: "Tell him that I did not leave him, and that I said he was ready," says the knight. "In the old days the dubbing was a true blow upon the neck, and now it is the flat of a sword upon the shoulder. Tell him to flinch at neither." He puts the sword into your hands hilt first, after the custom of knights, and it is hard for him to let it go.

thread.hint: Somewhere below, a squire still waits for his knight to catch up.

options.chronicle: Owe squire Tobyn Ser Brennan's sword. Tell him he was not left behind.

road.hint: You might bear a dying knight's sword to the squire who waits for it.

options.label: Sit with him
options.outcome: "Sit a little while, then, for I would not be alone at the end." You sit beside him through the longest minute of your life, and when it is over he is dead.
options.chronicle: Sat with Ser Brennan until he died.

road.hint: A dying knight may ask for nothing more than company at the end.

options.label: Take his sword and shield
options.outcome: He watches you lift the sword from his knees. "That is Tobyn's," he says. "I was saving it for Tobyn." But you are already walking away from him.
options.chronicle: Took dying Ser Brennan's sword and shield. The sword was meant for Tobyn.

road.hint: If you take a knight's sword, remember to whom it was promised.

name: Stone Statue
text: Statues fill the temple hall, a soldier with his sword half drawn, a dog, a shepherd with his crook, but one among them is wrong. A woman stands with an arm raised and her mouth open to scream, and her stone is newer than the rest, for this is the work of a basilisk. Beside her these words are scratched upon the wall: CELESTE. STONE BUT ALIVE. ANY SCROLL READ ALOUD, AND READ RIGHT, WILL WAKE HER. I WILL COME BACK FOR YOU. MAREN. Three rooms behind you lay the bones of a woman with a scroll case in her hand. The case was empty, and whatever scroll she had found, she was never able to read it. When you lean close against the stone you can feel, very faintly, the beating of a heart.

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the stair Celeste unbuckles the spare plate from her own pack. "Maren carried mine and I carried hers," she says, "and now it shall be yours."
on_arrive.chronicle: Saw Celeste safe to the stair. She would not speak of Maren.

on_fail.chronicle: Woke Celeste from stone, and lost her a floor later.

options.label: Read a scroll over the stone and restore her

pass.outcome: The stone cracks and falls, and Celeste gasps as her scream comes to its end. She reads the wall, and afterward she reads your face. "She tried," she says, and she goes back up the corridor alone to find what remains of Maren.
pass.chronicle: Woke Celeste from stone. She went to find her friend Maren's bones.

fail.outcome: You read too fast and the words tangle. With every slip a line of the scroll burns away, until the page is blank, and still the woman is stone and the heart beats on within her.
fail.chronicle: Misread the scroll over a stone woman. It burned blank. She is still stone.

road.hint: You might keep the promise that another made to a woman of stone.

options.label: Restore her, and walk the next floor down together

pass.outcome: At your reading the stone cracks and falls away. Celeste looks upon the wall and shuts her eyes. "Maren would wish me to finish the task," she says. "Walk a floor with me, and I will carry the torch."

fail.outcome: You read too fast and the words tangle. With every slip a line of the scroll burns away, until the page is blank, and still the woman is stone and the heart beats on within her.
fail.chronicle: Misread the scroll over a stone woman. It burned blank. She is still stone.

road.hint: One whom you wake from stone may know the dark, and walk it beside you.

options.label: Leave her as she is
options.outcome: You leave her as she is, and behind you the beating of her heart grows ever fainter as you go.
options.chronicle: Left a woman alive in stone. Her friend's bones lie three rooms back.

road.hint: A heart in stone beats long, but it will not beat for ever.

options.label: Break the statue to free her gear
options.outcome: The stone shatters, and what lived within it dies. The armour and the sword fall free unharmed, and you try not to look at such pieces as might have been a face.
options.chronicle: Broke a living statue for its armour. The heartbeat stopped.

road.hint: Some of the statues may be living still.

name: The Penitent

authority.why: A murderer answers to his victim's son and a lawful court.

text: A man kneels on the stone with his leg gashed by a fall upon the stair, and before him a dagger is laid down as a soldier surrenders his arms, with the hilt toward whoever comes. From a cord about his neck hangs a board with MURDERER burned into it by his own hand, and at his belt a heavy purse, untouched. "Twenty years ago I killed a man over money," he says, "and I have done with running." Behind you a younger man steps from the dark with a crossbow, and he does not lower it. "Tomas Dunmore was my father, and I was nine years old," he says. "I have tracked this man eleven years and twenty floors. He has fled from three assizes already, and each time it was because someone felt sorry for him. And now you would give him a potion?"

options.label: Heal his wound and let him go his way
options.warning: He has fled from three assizes already, and each time it was because someone felt sorry for him.
options.outcome: Lucan the murderer drinks, takes the board from his neck and is gone into the dark before young Aurel can resolve to shoot. The dead man's son looks long upon you. "Four," he says. "That makes four times."
options.chronicle: Healed Lucan the murderer. He fled. Four times now someone has let him go.

road.hint: A guilty man who is pitied and set free may flee from judgment again.

options.label: Weigh mercy and justice with them both

pass.outcome: You say it plainly, that mercy is no enemy of justice but follows after it, and that Lucan may live and still answer for Tomas Dunmore. Inch by inch Aurel lowers the crossbow. Then you heal the wound and show them both the stair, and you watch them climb, with the son walking behind the murderer.
pass.chronicle: Healed Lucan and handed him to his victim's son for the assize.

fail.outcome: You talk round and round forgiveness until Aurel can bear no more and departs. When you turn about, Lucan has slipped away into the dark and left the board lying behind him.
fail.chronicle: Failed to teach Lucan and Aurel mercy. They left by separate ways.

road.hint: A murderer might be shown mercy and still answer to justice.

options.label: "He was your father. You decide."
options.outcome: Aurel goes and looks down at him a long while. "I thought that I would feel something," he says, and he unloads the crossbow. "Let the dark have him, for it has waited long enough." He turns away, and Lucan watches him until he is gone.
options.chronicle: Let Aurel decide on his father's killer. He left Lucan to the dark.

road.hint: A son may forgo his vengeance, and justice be left undone.

options.label: Take his gold and the dagger
options.outcome: Lucan gives a cracked and dreadful laugh. "It suits you better than it suited me," he says, and Aurel watches you pocket the knife that slew his father and speaks no word at all.
options.chronicle: Took the murderer Lucan's purse and the knife he used.

road.hint: A murderer's knife is easy to take up, and heavy to carry afterward.

name: Young Knight
text: A young knight in armour bright as a mirror is searching room after room, and when he sees the shield you carry the colour leaves his face. "That is my father's, Ser Marten of the Iron Vale," he says. "He came down to clear a basilisk's nest in the old temple where the statues are, and he said that he would be back for supper." His voice breaks. "Tell me that he faced it." You have seen that the strap is cut through and that all the scrapes on its face run one way, as they would if the shield were dropped by a man running north, away from the nest.

options.label: Give him the shield and show him what the scrapes say
options.outcome: "Away from the nest," says Roderic, and for a space he is very still. "North of the nest is the camp, and in the camp were two squires and a cook." He takes up the shield. "He was running to warn them. He was running to warn them." He says it as one says a thing that he has resolved to believe, and you cannot tell him otherwise, for you do not know the truth of it yourself.
options.chronicle: Told Roderic the shield pointed from the nest. His father may have run for the camp.

road.hint: The truth that a shield tells may be kinder than you feared, or stranger.

options.label: Give him the shield and tell him his father died facing it
options.outcome: "Facing it," he says, and clasps the shield to his breast. "Of course he did, for he does not break his promises." He climbs the stair standing taller than when he came down, and bears with him a tale that he will tell to his mother, and one day to his children.
options.chronicle: Told Roderic his father died facing the basilisk. I do not know that.

road.hint: A kindly falsehood about a father may be handed down to his children.

options.label: Give him the shield and say nothing about the scrapes
options.outcome: He does not ask again. Perhaps he reads it in your face, or perhaps he has resolved not to. "Thank you," he says, and he bears the shield away as one bears a thing that is very heavy and very easily broken.
options.chronicle: Gave Roderic his father's shield. Said nothing of where it lay.

road.hint: If nothing is said, a son must read his father's end as best he can.

options.label: Keep the shield, and say why: "I need it to get down alive. If I live, it comes home."
options.outcome: Roderic looks at the shield and at the stair, and in that moment he resolves to be his father's son. "Then carry it well," he says. "He would wish it used rather than hung upon a wall." He tells you the road to the Iron Vale and the name of his mother, so that when you come to her she will know who you are.
options.chronicle: Owe Ser Marten's shield to Roderic's mother in the Iron Vale, if I live.

road.hint: The shield of the dead might be borrowed, if his heir agreed to the loan.

name: Dying Courier
text: A young man in a courier's jerkin lies upon his side with a crossbow bolt in his back, and his hand is stretched toward an iron scroll case, sealed by the Watch, that is just out of reach. "It is for Sergeant Holt at the post on the lower stair," he says, "to say which gates to hold." His fingers scrape the stone. "The Watch holds those gates so that nothing coming up the stair reaches the city's wells, and if they guess wrong thousands will die up there. Please take it down. Swear to me that you will." You see that he lies awkwardly, upon something lumpy beneath his hip.

options.label: Take the dispatch and swear to carry it down

oath.what: Carry the Watch dispatch down to Sergeant Holt's post.

options.outcome: The case goes into your pack, and he smiles and closes his eyes. "Tell them that Edric made it almost all the way," he says.

thread.hint: Somewhere below, a Watch sergeant still waits for her orders.

options.chronicle: Swore to dying Edric to carry his dispatch down. Say he almost made it.

road.hint: A promise sworn to the dying must be kept, for none can release you.

outcome_variants.outcome: You take the case from beside the dead man and swear it to him none the less, so that someone may tell how he made it almost all the way.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Swore over a dead courier, Edric, to carry his dispatch down. Say he almost made it.

options.label: Turn him over and look at the wound

pass.outcome: The bolt is lodged in the muscle, a thumb's breadth from the spine, and under his hip, where he fell upon it, lies his own healing draught, which he never knew was there. You draw the bolt and pour the draught, and Edric sits up with the look of one betrayed by his own good luck. "I'll run it down myself," he says, "and you tell nobody that I fainted."

delayed.text: On the stair a purse of the Watch hangs from a nail, and beside it these words are chalked: E.F., ALL THE WAY.
delayed.chronicle: Found Edric's purse on the stair. He made it all the way.

pass.chronicle: Found Edric's own draught under him. He lived, and took his dispatch on.

fail.outcome: As you turn him the bolt shifts. He gasps once and dies, and the scroll case still lies waiting upon the stone.
fail.chronicle: Botched a look at the courier's wound. He died. His dispatch still waits.

road.hint: A dying man may be lying on the very thing that would save him.

options.label: Tell him you cannot promise
options.outcome: "I understand. Only, if you should see anyone else," he says, and his voice fails him. The case lies on the stone between you, and you step around it.
options.chronicle: Would not promise to carry a dying courier's dispatch. Left it.

road.hint: A dispatch left on the floor will never reach its sergeant.

options.label: Take his purse and whatever he's lying on. Leave the case
options.outcome: All along his healing draught was pinned beneath his hip. You take it, and his hazard pay with it, and he watches you step over the scroll case. "Thousands," he whispers.
options.chronicle: Took a dying courier's pay and draught as he watched. Left his dispatch.

road.hint: The purse of a dying man may be bought too dearly.

outcome_variants.outcome: His healing draught was pinned beneath his hip all along. His hand does not stir as you take the draught and his hazard pay. Then you step over the scroll case and go on your way.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Took a dead courier's pay and draught, unseen. Left his dispatch.

options.label: Leave the case where it lies
options.outcome: You close his eyes. The case lies on the stone beside him, where he could never reach it, and you step around it and go on your way.
options.chronicle: Moved Edric wrongly and he died. Left his dispatch beside him.

road.hint: The case that is left beside the dead will lie where it fell.

name: Sister Marguerite
text: A nun whose habit has turned grey kneels beside a monk who will not rise again, and at his neck hangs a silver reliquary with a saint's fingerbone in a cage of gold. "Brother Cormac has borne Saint Columba from Iona," she says, "and I gave away our bread to all whom we met." She smiles as though at a jest. "There is a chapel below where the brothers keep the stair, and the saint was meant to lie there, but I cannot carry both Cormac and the relic." The gold would sell for a year of ease, or it might rest warm against your own breast.

options.label: Swear to carry the reliquary to the chapel

oath.what: Lay Saint Columba's relic in the Chapel of the Deep Watch.

options.outcome: She lifts it from Cormac's neck, and she kisses his forehead first and afterward the gold. "It is warm when it is worn," she says, "and you must not let that persuade you."

thread.hint: Somewhere below, an empty niche above an altar is waiting for a saint.

options.chronicle: Must take Saint Columba's finger to a chapel for Sister Marguerite. Warm if worn.

road.hint: A relic may be worn upon the road, but it is not yours to keep.

options.label: Give them food
options.outcome: She eats half and feeds the rest to Cormac crumb by crumb, though he can swallow no longer. "You have fed Christ's servants, the both of us," she says. "He will remember it." Then she makes ready to carry the saint down herself, however slowly she must go.
options.chronicle: Fed Sister Marguerite and a dying monk.

road.hint: With bread to eat, a nun might bear the relic down herself.

options.label: Take the reliquary to wear
options.outcome: She is too weary to hinder you. "Then wear it well," she says, "and remember whose finger it was."
options.chronicle: Took a saint's finger off a dying monk. It is warm to the touch.

road.hint: A saint's bone will be holy still, though a thief should wear it.

options.label: Leave them to their prayers
options.outcome: She folds Cormac's hands over the reliquary and, all alone, begins to say the Office for the Dead.
options.chronicle: Left Sister Marguerite saying the Office over her brother monk.

road.hint: A nun's prayer is heard, though she prays alone.

name: Slaver's Coffle
stance_note: Steel-man: Aristotle's natural-slavery argument and Rusk's "who feeds him if I don't" are in the scene at full strength. The answer is Theodoros's one line, and the lean is carried by the karma, not a speech.
text: Four captives go chained neck to neck in a coffle, the last of them a grey-bearded man too old to keep the pace, and a cage is slung upon two poles for when he falls. A big man in a good coat leans on the poles. "Domnall Rusk, an honest trader," he says, and he points to the greybeard. "That is Theodoros, who reads six languages. Aristotle, whose books your schools teach, says that some men are slaves by nature. His own city sold him for a debt, and it is I who feed him. Set him free and he starves in the first ditch, so who is the crueller?" Theodoros answers without looking up, "I can read his contract. It says I am a thing."

options.label: Buy Theodoros and strike his chains, haggling hard

pass.outcome: You find the flaw in his price, for a scholar is worth nothing to one who cannot sell him before the next floor. Rusk swears and hands back half, and with his own hammer you strike off the chains. Theodoros reads your face as he would read a page. "I will repay this," he says, "in the only coin that I have."

delayed.text: A scroll case waits for you on the stair, and with it a note in six languages, each of which says the same thing.

pass.chronicle: Haggled well, bought Theodoros from the slaver and freed him.

fail.outcome: Rusk knows his trade better than you know yours, and you pay the whole of his price, yet you strike off the chains for all that. Theodoros rubs his wrists. "You have overpaid," he says, "and I thank you."

delayed.text: A scroll case waits for you on the stair, and with it a note in six languages, each of which says the same thing.

fail.chronicle: Paid the slaver full price to free Theodoros the scholar.

road.hint: A scholar who reads his own contract might be bought only to be freed.

options.label: Attack Rusk and free all four
options.outcome: Rusk reaches for the axe at his belt, and while he is drawing it you strike through the coffle chain, with Theodoros to help you. The two sisters run off without a word, as well they may. The goatherd boy takes Rusk's hat, and Theodoros takes the boy's hand. "I can read the signs upon the stair," he says, "and we shall go up together, but look to yourself now, for Rusk is upon you."
options.chronicle: Fought the slaver Rusk and freed his whole coffle.

road.hint: A slaver might be fought for all his captives.

options.label: Buy Theodoros to carry your pack
options.outcome: Rusk shakes your hand. While you sign the bill of sale Theodoros reads it aloud in a toneless voice, every word, and then he shoulders your pack and says nothing at all.
options.chronicle: Bought Theodoros from a slaver to carry my pack.

road.hint: A porter who reads six languages will remember how he was bought.

delayed.text: For five floors Theodoros has carried everything and said nothing at all. Now, at a change of the watch, you find that he is gone, and with him your second-best knife.
delayed.chronicle: Theodoros, the man I bought, fled with my second-best knife.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Rusk tips his hat to you, and Theodoros returns to his reading of the bars.
options.chronicle: Walked past a slaver's coffle. One man in it was reading.

road.hint: The coffle will go on in chains if none helps.

name: Ghost of Hal
text: At the foot of a wall lies a cairn of piled stones, and scratched above it are the words HERE LIES EDWIN. HE DESERVED BETTER. A broad-shouldered ghost stands guard there, with the sting that killed him still in his body. "He was my partner seven years," says the ghost, and he looks at you, "and he pushed me behind him when it came. I buried him with no priest and no prayer, and the dead cannot bless the dead. Will you keep the vigil for him? It will take something out of you, and I will not lie to you about that." Between the stones you catch the glint of a soldier's stash.

options.label: Keep the vigil and say the prayers for the dead
options.outcome: You kneel and say every word that you remember, while the cold climbs into you, and some of it stays. The stones grow warm. "I thank you," says Hal the ghost. "Now we can both go." And he passes into the light as a man passes into a warm room.

outcome_variants.outcome: You kneel and say every word that you remember, while the cold climbs into you, and some of it stays. The stones grow warm. "Tell him that I came back," says Hal, "too late, but I came back." You give Edwin the message, and afterward the two depart together.

options.chronicle: Kept vigil at Edwin's cairn. Hal's ghost rests. It took something for good.

road.hint: The living may bless the dead, though the vigil has its price.

options.label: Ask him why Edwin deserved better
options.outcome: Hal is long silent. "It is because he pushed me behind him and I ran," he says. "I came back when it was done. That is why I cannot bless him, and my being dead has little to do with it."

options.label: Bow your head and tell him you cannot stay
options.outcome: "Not everyone can," he says, and turns to the cairn. "I'll stand here and I don't mind it, for he is worth standing for."
options.chronicle: Would not keep Hal's vigil. His ghost still guards the cairn.

road.hint: A ghost may stand his watch with no relief.

options.label: Take the stash from the cairn
options.outcome: You pull the stones apart. The ghost does not rage, but says very softly, "That was his grave," and kneels to set the stones in their places again, though his hands pass through every one.
options.chronicle: Robbed Edwin's cairn while Hal's ghost watched.

road.hint: A soldier's cairn may have a guard, though it be only his dead friend.

name: Legion Deserter
text: In the darkness beside the way sits a young soldier of the Legion with his tabard torn, and upon a cord at his neck hangs a captain's heavy signet, too great for any finger of his. He trembles as he lifts his face to you. "We came down a hundred strong," he says, "and something rose against us out of the dark, and I fled from it. Sergeant Ormond brought some of the men into the old granary below, and I heard the bar fall across the door as I ran. Give me only food enough to reach the sunlight, and I will trouble no one again." You see that there is no blood upon his sword or upon his tabard. It is plain to you that he struck no blow before he fled.

options.label: Give him food for the climb
options.warning: You see that there is no blood upon his sword or upon his tabard.
options.outcome: He eats as one who has long gone hungry, until shame comes upon him and he lays the rest aside, and then he thanks you in a low voice and climbs away toward the light. Far beneath you, behind a barred door, eleven men still wait for help, and the one who might have brought it to them has taken the upward road.
options.chronicle: Fed Pell, a deserter. His company is trapped in the granary below.

road.hint: One who flees may have left comrades in need of him.

options.label: Tell him about the Spartan who came home from Thermopylae

pass.outcome: You tell him of Aristodemus the Spartan, who was sent home sick from Thermopylae and for a year was shamed among his people with the name of Trembler, and who came afterward to the next great battle and fought there more bravely than any other. Pell listens as one who hears his own tale told, and at the end of it he rises and takes up his sword. "The granary lies a few floors below us," he says, "and I know the road to it."
pass.chronicle: Told Pell of the Spartan who came back. He went back to his company.

fail.outcome: You begin the tale, but in your telling it becomes a sermon upon duty, and he finds no comfort in it. Pell hears you courteously to the end, and then, taking nothing from you, he turns and climbs the stair as swiftly as he is able.
fail.chronicle: Preached at Pell, a deserter. He ran on uphill.

road.hint: An old tale may give a frightened soldier the heart to turn back.

options.label: Point him toward the stairs and keep your food
options.outcome: "Yes," he answers softly, and asks nothing more of you. He rises like one who walks in an evil dream and sets out along the passage you have shown him, toward the world above.
options.chronicle: Sent Pell upstairs unfed. A barred granary waits somewhere below.

road.hint: A frightened man will take whatever road he is shown.

options.label: Demand the officer's signet
options.outcome: "Take it, for I have no right to it," he says, and draws the cord over his head. "It was Captain Dorn's, and I took it from him when he fell." He gives it up willingly, and as it passes into your keeping you find it heavier than so small a thing should be.
options.chronicle: Took dead Captain Dorn's signet from Pell.

road.hint: A captain's ring may still carry his orders after his death.

name: Quarrelling Dwarves
text: On either side of an iron chest stand a dwarf woman and her brother, alike in their soot-black brows, and each has a hand upon the lid. Frida, the elder, has the look of one who has not taken her hand away for days. "Father left his gold to the one who stayed with him," she says, "and it was I who stayed." Hepti, who is a smith by his burned forearms, does not raise his voice. "Father left it to us both, and she has not once slept off that chest since we buried him." Between the chest and the water barrel, where Frida must walk to drink, a long trench has been dug in the floor and roofed over with planks and a skin of dust.

options.label: Split the gold between them, here and now
options.warning: Between the chest and the water barrel, where Frida must walk to drink, a long trench has been dug in the floor and roofed over with planks and a skin of dust.
options.outcome: You count it out coin for coin upon the lid while they both watch your hands, and though the shares come out even, each looks cheated. Hepti thanks you a little too warmly. On the stair you hear the crack of planks, with a short cry after it, and by the sound of a shovel you know that Frida has fallen and that her brother is filling in the pit.
options.chronicle: Split a smith's gold between Frida and Hepti. Missed the pit he dug for her.

road.hint: An even share will not content a brother who has already dug a pit.

options.label: Tell them what Hreidmar's gold did to his children

pass.outcome: You tell it as the skalds tell it. Loki killed an otter with a stone, and it was Otr, the son of the dwarf Hreidmar, so that the gods had to pay for him in gold enough to fill his skin and cover it, and upon the last whisker they laid the cursed ring of the dwarf Andvari. Hreidmar would not share a coin with his other sons. For this Fafnir slew him, and lay upon the gold until he became the worm below, and Regin taught a boy to dig a pit in the path of that worm, who was his own brother. Hepti looks long upon the trench that he has made. Then he takes up a shovel and begins to fill it, and Frida lifts her hand from the lid.
pass.chronicle: Told Frida and Hepti of Hreidmar's sons. The pit is filled, and they share.

fail.outcome: You tangle the tale of the otter and the ring and which brother did what. Frida laughs at you, though Hepti does not, and you leave them as you found them, with their hands upon the lid.
fail.chronicle: Botched the tale of Hreidmar's gold. Frida and Hepti still quarrel.

road.hint: The tale of a cursed hoard might turn brother and sister from their feud.

options.label: Side with Hepti, for a third of the gold
options.outcome: Hepti nods, as if he had expected it of you. That night you hold the lamp while Frida walks toward the water barrel and into the pit. Afterward he fills in the trench himself, and he counts your third of the gold out twice.
options.chronicle: Held the lamp as Frida walked into Hepti's pit. Got a third of the gold.

road.hint: Gold paid for holding a lamp while another dies is blood money still.

options.label: Leave them to their chest
options.outcome: Neither of them looks up at your going, and behind you no hand is moved from the lid.
options.chronicle: Left Frida and Hepti at the chest. There was a trench in the floor.

road.hint: A covered trench across a path was dug for the one who walks there.

name: Blind Seer
text: From an iron hook hangs a bottle, and within it sits a woman no bigger than a sparrow, so old that her skin is like paper folded too many times. On the floor beneath lie three books, beside a heap of ash where six others were. "I had nine books of all that is to come," she whispers, "and a king would not pay my price. So I burned three and asked the same price for six, and then I burned three more." She turns her eyes upon the last three. "The price is still the same."

options.label: Pay her price for the last three books
options.outcome: She does not count it, for she could not lift a coin. "King Tarquin paid as much for three in the end," she says, "and he wept for the six as long as he lived." The books are warm to your hand, and in one of them you find your name already written.
options.chronicle: Bought the bottled Sibyl's last three books of prophecy.

road.hint: Some sellers will burn their wares before they will lower the price.

options.label: Haggle

pass.outcome: As you look upon the ash you understand that it is no paper she sells, but the last of a thing that will not come again, and so you pay at once, before the same price can buy any fewer books. She is well pleased, and she gives you the page that she tore long ago out of the first book.
pass.chronicle: Paid the Sibyl unargued. Got the page she kept back from a king.

fail.outcome: While you haggle she looks upon one of the books, and it begins to smoulder on the floor. "The price is the same," she says.
fail.chronicle: Haggled with the Sibyl. She burned a book and kept the price.

road.hint: A wise buyer pays the Sibyl before another of her books is burned.

options.label: Ask her what she wants
options.outcome: "When the boys came to the jar in Cumae they asked me that also," she says, and the tiny face creases. "I want to die. I asked for years of life and forgot to ask for youth. Do not fall into my error, but ask for the whole of what you want."
options.chronicle: The Sibyl has wished to die for a thousand years. I could not help.

road.hint: Ask the old seer her wish, and learn to ask for the whole of your own.

options.label: Leave her be
options.outcome: "Everyone leaves me," she says, "and it is the one thing that I can foretell without the books."
options.chronicle: Left the Sibyl on her hook, as she foretold.

road.hint: The Sibyl needs no book to foretell who will leave her.

name: Caged Angel
text: In a cage of black iron kneels a winged figure with six wings folded against bars too narrow for them, and the air smells of lightning and wildflowers. Beside the cage a neat man in grey sits on a folding stool, with a ledger that writes in itself as he talks. He has not blinked since you came in, and his chest neither rises nor falls. "Ambrose Vell, acquisitions," he says. "She is lawfully bought and paid for." He taps a deed with a red seal. "I will pay you a finder's fee to keep walking." Against the far wall lean two trolls in Vell's grey livery, picking their teeth with arrows. The angel speaks softly, and says no more than this: "A scroll would break it."

options.label: Break the cage with a scroll, here and now
options.warning: Against the far wall lean two trolls in Vell's grey livery, picking their teeth with arrows.
options.outcome: The bars burst in white light, and Sariel the angel rises upon nine feet of wings and is gone. The trolls were paid to guard the stock, and now that the stock has flown they turn to guarding you instead.
options.chronicle: Broke Sariel the angel from her cage. Had to fight the trolls.

road.hint: Mark well who is standing guard before you break open the cage.

options.label: Ask to read Vell's deed of sale

pass.outcome: The deed is grand and sealed and signed "Mammon, Prince of This World", but it is written in schoolboy Latin with every other case wrong. You read it aloud slowly, faults and all, until the trolls look at one another, for they were promised lawful work, and they depart. Vell will not argue with an empty room, and between two fingers he hands you the key. "Seven seals hold shut what lies below, and a keeper stands upon each," says Sariel the angel as you set her free. "I will not forget."

delayed.text: Across the stair lies a white feather, and it is warm to your hand.

pass.chronicle: Found Vell's deed of sale forged. The angel went free.

fail.outcome: To your eyes it seems a true deed. Vell smiles and folds it away. "Good day to you," he says, and the angel closes her eyes.
fail.chronicle: Found no fault in Vell's deed. The angel stays caged.

road.hint: A forged deed may betray itself by its faulty spelling.

options.label: Take Vell's finder's fee
options.outcome: Vell counts it out coin by coin and enters you in his ledger under Associates. The angel does not look at you, and it would be easier to bear if she did.
options.chronicle: Took Vell's money to forget a caged angel. He lists me as an associate.

road.hint: Whoever takes Vell's fee is entered in his ledger.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "That is wise of you," says Vell without looking up, and behind you a cart is coming down the stair to fetch the cage.
options.chronicle: Walked past an angel in Vell's cage.

road.hint: A caged captive will be carted off if none helps.

name: Deacon on the Gridiron
text: Upon an iron gridiron over the coals a man in a deacon's scorched tunic sits as on a garden bench, and is not burned. About him crouch nine thin people with chain-galls on their necks, and a clinking sack between their feet. "I am Lawrence, a deacon of Rome," he says. "The prefect once asked me for the Church's treasures, so I took three days, gave every coin to the poor, and brought him the poor. 'These are the treasures of the Church,' I told him, and he put me on this for it. As the story goes, I told him to turn me over, for I was done on that side." He nods at the nine. "They fled the dwarves' chain-gangs with their masters' gold. Walk them to the up-stair and it is yours, for they would rather be alive than rich." Somewhere below, some great thing is following their scent.

on_arrive.outcome: At the stair Agnes counts the gold into your hands unasked, and she does not look sorry to part with it. The nine climb the steps into the dark above, and none of them looks behind.
on_arrive.chronicle: Saw nine chain-gang runaways to the up-stair. Took the gold offered.

on_fail.chronicle: Lost the nine chain-gang runaways. Something tracked them by smell.

on_arrive.outcome: At the stair Agnes tries even so to give you the sack, and you close her hands upon it. The nine climb the steps into the dark above, bearing their road home between them.
on_arrive.chronicle: Saw nine chain-gang runaways to the up-stair. Left them the gold for home.

on_fail.chronicle: Lost the nine chain-gang runaways. Something tracked them by smell.

options.label: Walk them to the up-stair, and take the gold as your wage
options.outcome: "I am Agnes," says the eldest of the nine, and she sets the others moving, while Lawrence lifts two fingers in blessing over you all as you go.

road.hint: An honest wage may be taken, or as honestly refused.

options.label: Walk them to the up-stair, and leave them the gold for their road home
options.outcome: Lawrence laughs, and it is a great laugh for a man upon a gridiron. "Now that is the treasure of the Church!" he says. Agnes, the eldest of the nine, sets the others moving, and she keeps one hand upon the sack.

road.hint: The poor who carried out their treasure might keep it for their road home.

options.label: Find them the cool way up, by the draught

pass.outcome: You wet a finger and hold it low and afterward high. The coals warm the air and it rises, and cool air creeps in along the floor from the way out to take its place, as it does in any cave that has two mouths. At the height of your ankle you follow the draught to a crack that opens on the up-stair, and the nine climb by it with their sack, and nothing follows them. Lawrence blesses you with two fingers. "A geographer!" he says. "The prefect never had one of those."
pass.chronicle: Found the nine a safe way up by the draught. The deacon blessed me.

fail.outcome: The draught that you follow is the breath of something lying in the dark, and it wakes. As it rises the nine flee up some other passage, and Lawrence goes with them, leaving you to face it.
fail.chronicle: The draught led to a troll. The nine found their own way out.

road.hint: Warm air rises, and the cool draught that replaces it shows the way out.

options.label: Wish them luck and go on
options.outcome: "God speed you, then," says Lawrence with all his heart, and the nine watch you as you go.
options.chronicle: Left nine souls, the Church's treasure, to the deacon on the gridiron.

road.hint: The deacon counts nine fugitives as the treasure of the Church.

name: Cursed Scholar
text: Before you stands a man whose hands are fused to a book. Veins of black light climb his arms, his eyes are wholly void, and his lips whisper in a tongue that makes your teeth ache, until for a moment the man himself looks out. "Kill the book, but spare me," he says. "I was a schoolmaster, and I had a wife named Clara. My feet have not been my own since the second floor, for it walked me down here to find someone who would read it." His voice breaks. "I cannot remember her face, for it took that first." The book's iron clasp is shaped like a mouth, and it is smiling. The words that bind it run round the cover, and they are written backwards.

options.label: Read the binding words backwards, staking your own wits

pass.outcome: Writing backwards is an old craft, for in such mirror script, from right to left, Leonardo da Vinci kept his notebooks, which none could read without a mirror or much patience. With a like patience you read the binding backwards, clause by clause, until the grammar folds in upon itself like a closing hand and the book lets go of him. Ewan the schoolmaster looks up with eyes that are blue. "Clara," he says. "Her eyes are brown. I remember now that they are brown."
pass.chronicle: Read the binding backwards and freed Ewan the schoolmaster.

fail.outcome: Halfway through you lose the thread, and the book finds it. Black light runs up your wrists, and the thing takes a bite of you and keeps the man. The whispering begins again, and for a while some of it is within your own head.
fail.chronicle: Failed to read Ewan free. The book kept him and wounded me.

road.hint: A curse that is written backwards might be undone by reading it rightly.

options.label: Rip the book out of his hands
options.warning: The book's iron clasp is shaped like a mouth, and it is smiling.
options.outcome: The book comes away, taking the skin of his palms with it, and the clasp bites your wrist as it passes. Ewan is free, but he screams with the pain, and he will never hold a pen again, while the book lies upon the floor, smiling at nothing.
options.chronicle: Tore the cursed book from Ewan. He lives, but will never write again.

road.hint: The swiftest cure may free a man and yet not leave him whole.

options.label: Pull the book free and read it yourself
options.outcome: The clasp bites you as it passes, but you do not care, for already you are reading. Forbidden knowledge floods into you, the dark scholarship of centuries and the true names of things that should have stayed nameless. When you lift your eyes the schoolmaster lies upon the floor still breathing, and he is no more than a hollow and empty shell.
options.chronicle: Read the book that ate Ewan. He breathes, and that is all.

road.hint: Forbidden lore may be paid for by the one who held the book before you.

options.label: Back away from the book
options.outcome: The human moment passes. His eyes grow black once more and the whispering begins again, and the man who spoke to you is gone.
options.chronicle: Left Ewan to the cursed book. He has forgotten his wife, Clara.

road.hint: A man who begs you to kill his book has need of one who will stay.

name: Trapped Fairy
text: A tiny winged woman is shut in a jar of thick glass with wax and iron wire, and the dust of her broken wings coats the inside like frost. She presses both hands to the glass. "I have been here eight months," she says, "and the dust is my wings. If I had it back, I could mend them." A neat man in grey is already reaching for the jar. The cave is so cold that your breath shows, yet his does not show at all. "Ambrose Vell, acquisitions," he says. "I will buy her, or, if you are squeamish, you may let her go and sell me the dust. It is only on the glass, and she has shed it." It is plain that he means both offers, and that his purse is heavy.
