options.label: Sell her to Vell
options.outcome: Vell tucks the jar beneath his arm like a loaf. Tansy, for that is the fairy's name, has ceased to beat upon the glass. She watches you count the coins, and she does not look away until he has turned the corner.
options.chronicle: Sold Tansy, a fairy in a jar, to Ambrose Vell.

road.hint: The price of a captive in a jar is paid by the captive herself.

options.label: Let her go, and sell Vell the dust
options.outcome: You break the wax and she tumbles out gasping. With a little silver spoon Vell scrapes the glass clean into a silken bag, pinch by pinch, while she watches from the floor. Her wings are still bent. "That was my flying," she says, and she limps away into the dark on foot.
options.chronicle: Freed Tansy but sold Vell her dust. She cannot fly now.

road.hint: The dust that a fairy has shed may still belong to her.

options.label: Let her go, and give her back the dust
options.outcome: You shatter the jar and tip the glass toward her. The dust lifts from it as frost lifts from a window in the sun and settles again into her wings, and you see that it was never dust at all, but thousands of scales, laid like the slates of a roof, the same as on the wing of a moth. Her wings straighten with the sound of a turning page. She flies a loop about your head and kisses your cheek, leaving a warm spot no bigger than a pinprick, and Vell closes his purse with a small sigh.

delayed.text: A ring of tiny mushrooms has sprung up on the stair, and in the midst of it stands a thimble of something golden.

options.chronicle: Freed Tansy and refused Vell's gold for her dust. She flies again.

road.hint: A fairy has a long memory, and may leave a gift in a ring of mushrooms.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: As you go upon your way, Vell picks up the jar behind you.
options.chronicle: Left Tansy's jar to Ambrose Vell.

road.hint: The jar that is left behind will go into the collector's cart.

name: The Bound One and His Wife
text: In a cave of black ice a man lies bound across three stones with cords that have turned to iron, and over his face a great serpent hangs from the roof and drips its venom. At his head kneels a woman, whose arms tremble as she holds a bowl beneath the drip. "I am Sigyn, his wife," she says, before you can ask. Whenever the bowl is full she must turn away to empty it, and then the venom falls upon his face and he writhes until the whole floor shakes. The bound man turns his eyes upon you, and they are bright with amusement. "Cut but one cord," says Loki, "and I will make you a thing that nobody has ever made. It was I who invented the net, you know."

options.label: Ask Sigyn why she stays

pass.outcome: "Because he is mine," she says, "and the gods made sure that I would see what he did." She tells it simply. Loki put a dart of mistletoe in the hand of blind Hod and aimed it at Baldr, whom nothing else in the world could harm. Afterward, when all things wept to bring Baldr back from Hel, one old giantess in a cave would not, and men say that she was Loki. Therefore the gods bound him here with his own son's cords until the end of the world. "When the ice breaks he will break loose, and it will be Ragnarok, so go down ready," she says, and she wipes your hands with something from a little jar. "His venom will not trouble you for a while." Then she looks at the bowl and at her trembling arms, and for the first time she truly looks at you.
pass.chronicle: Loki breaks loose when the ice breaks. Have Sigyn's aid against his venom.

fail.outcome: She looks at you for a long while and says nothing at all, and as the bowl fills behind her she turns back to her task.
fail.chronicle: Asked Sigyn why she stays by Loki. She would not answer.

road.hint: The bound god talks much, but his wife knows the whole of the tale.

options.label: Refuse him, and hold the bowl so Sigyn can rest
options.outcome: You take the bowl, which is heavier than it looks, and every drop that misses it eats into your hands. Sigyn empties it, and then she sleeps against the wall for the first time in longer than you care to reckon. All the while Loki talks, sweetly at first and afterward cruelly, until at last he falls silent. When she wakes she takes back the bowl without a word, and her hands have ceased to tremble.
options.chronicle: Held Sigyn's bowl while she slept. Refused Loki's bargain.

road.hint: The wife who holds the bowl might rest, if another held it for a while.

options.label: Cut one cord, for his gift
options.outcome: The cord parts like rotten rope, and Loki laughs long in his delight while the floor heaves beneath you. He keeps his word after a fashion, for something lies in your pack that was not there before, but Sigyn will not look at you.
options.chronicle: Cut one of Loki's cords for a gift. He laughed and the floor shook.

road.hint: Think whom the maker of nets would catch, before you take his gift.

options.label: Leave them to their long night
options.outcome: Loki calls after you pleasantly as far as the turn of the passage, and twice before you reach the stair you feel the floor shake.
options.chronicle: Left Loki and Sigyn under the serpent. The floor shook twice after.

road.hint: The ground will shake whenever Sigyn's bowl is full.

name: Forgotten Prisoner
text: The cell is ancient, its bars are more rust than iron, and within it sits a white-haired man as pleasant as a grandfather. "Forty-three years I have been here, and for a debt, if you can believe it," he says. He talks of chains, and of how iron is the weaker sort, since the one that holds the great wolf is as soft as a ribbon. "The lock is of dwarven make, and gold in the works will trip it." The wall behind him is covered in scratches, but these were not made to tally the days. They're too long, and each has a little cross after it. Beneath his cot, within reach of the bars, one flagstone stands a little proud of the rest.

options.label: Feed your gold into the lock
options.warning: They're too long, and each has a little cross after it.
options.outcome: The lock groans and swings open. He stands for the first time in forty-three years, and when his knees buckle you catch him, and he holds to you longer than he has need. Then he presses a little stoppered flask into your hand. "It is for the road," he says, "for you have been so very kind."

delayed.text: In a cistern on the stair a dead rat is floating, and you see that someone has scratched a little cross upon the rim.

options.chronicle: Paid to free an old prisoner. He gave me a flask. Have not drunk it.

road.hint: Read a prisoner's wall before you open his door.

options.label: Read the scratches before you decide

pass.outcome: They are names and no count of days: the household of Duke Osbert of Morvane, eleven of them, the Duke first and the wet nurse last, and by each a little cross. "A debt," he says, as he watches you read. "I said a debt and I meant it, for it was they who owed me."
pass.chronicle: Prisoner's wall bears eleven names, eleven crosses. He called it a debt.

fail.outcome: The scratches mean nothing to you. He watches you and smiles as kindly as any grandfather.

road.hint: Forty-three years cannot undo what is written on a prisoner's wall.

options.label: Leave him to his sentence
options.outcome: He shrugs. "It has been forty-three years, and what are forty more?" he says. Then he returns to his wall and begins very neatly to scratch your name.
options.chronicle: Left the killer of eleven in his cell. He is adding my name to his wall.

road.hint: However long a sentence has run, it may not have paid the debt.

options.label: Free him anyway, knowing
options.outcome: He walks out without a word, and he neither tries to touch you nor offers you anything at all to drink.
options.chronicle: Freed the poisoner after forty-three years, knowing what he was.

road.hint: Mercy may be given with open eyes, though the risk remains.

options.label: Tell him you cannot afford it
options.outcome: "No one can. I've had forty-three years of no one being able to afford it." He folds his hands and says, "Perhaps the next one."
options.chronicle: Could not pay the old prisoner's lock. Never learned why he is held.

road.hint: It may be cheaper to leave an old lock shut.

options.label: Reach through the bars for his hidden cache
options.outcome: "That is all I have," he says very calmly, and he watches your hand and says no more. Some while afterward your fingertips begin to itch where you touched the coins.
options.chronicle: Robbed the old prisoner's cache. Beware those coins, my fingers itch.

road.hint: An old poisoner will have tended his savings as he did his wine.

name: Valkyrie by the Lake
text: By a black lake under the ice a woman in a shirt of ring-mail sits upon a stone with a spear across her knees, and her eyes never leave a heap of white feathers in the lap of a frost giant, who is fast asleep and snoring. "That is my swan-shirt," she says. "I am Hrist, one of Odin's choosers of the slain. Whoever holds that shirt holds me, so that I must fly where he bids, and on the day of battle choose for whom he bids. The giant does not know it." At last she turns her eyes upon you. "But now you know it."

options.label: Take the shirt from the giant, and keep it
options.outcome: You lift it from the sleeping giant, as light as breath, and Hrist stands because she must. "Where you go, then, I go," she says, in a voice without any colour. For a while a spear goes before you and every blow you strike finds its mark. But there comes a morning when the shirt is gone from your pack, and Hrist has departed with it and bidden you no farewell.
options.chronicle: Kept Hrist's swan-shirt to bind her. She fought for me, then took it.

road.hint: A chooser of the slain will remember who took away her choice.

options.label: Take the shirt from the giant, and give it back to her
options.outcome: The giant wakes with his fist closed about the feathers, but you are the quicker, and you drag them free and cast the shirt to her. She draws it on and is a swan, and then a woman again, laughing, as the giant heaves himself up against you. "It was freely given," she says, "and I will remember that on the day of choosing."
options.chronicle: Fought for Hrist's swan-shirt and returned it. She will recall it at the choosing.

road.hint: A swan-shirt might be won and given back to its owner.

options.label: Wake him, and win it off him in a riddle game

pass.outcome: You wake him courteously and offer a wager of riddles for the shirt. No giant ever refused a riddle game, and this one is slow of wit, so that he loses the third round, pays with a bad grace and lies down again to sleep. Hrist takes the shirt from your hands. "Valkyrie means chooser of the slain," she says. "Of those we choose, half go to Odin's hall to fight at Ragnarok and half to Freyja. You could have kept me, and you knew it." With that she becomes a swan and flies away over the lake.
pass.chronicle: Won Hrist's swan-shirt back at riddles. She is a chooser of the slain.

fail.outcome: Your first riddle has an answer that he knows, and his has one that you do not, so that he roars and comes upon you. Even then Hrist herself plucks the shirt out of his fist, and she is away over the lake before you can turn.
fail.chronicle: Lost at riddles and fought the giant. Hrist took back her own shirt.

road.hint: No giant refuses a riddle game, though few giants ever won one.

options.label: Leave the giant to his sleep
options.outcome: Hrist never takes her eyes from the feathers as you go, and the giant snores on in his sleep.
options.chronicle: Left Hrist by the lake. A sleeping giant still has her swan-shirt.

road.hint: While the giant sleeps on, he will keep the thing he holds.

name: Thrym's Wedding Feast
text: The tables groan in a frost giant's hall, where Thrym, lord of the rime-giants, sits beside a veiled bride as tall as a door. "It is Freyja herself!" he booms. "I hid the Thunderer's hammer eight leagues under the earth, and she was the price of it." The bride has just eaten an ox, eight salmon and every dainty that was meant for the women, and has washed them down with three casks of mead. Beneath the veil her eyes burn like coals. Her bridesmaid, a lean red-haired girl with old stitch-scars round her mouth, catches your eye and does not blink. Thrym turns to you, a little troubled in his mind. "Stranger," he says, "did you ever see a bride eat like that?"

options.label: Tell Thrym the truth: that is no bride
options.outcome: Thrym tears away the veil and finds a red beard beneath it. He roars for the hammer to be buried deeper still, and bride and maid are cast out into the snow, the bride swearing like a storm, though once, as she goes, the bridesmaid looks back at you. Then Thrym fills your hands with gold for the sharpness of your eyes.
options.chronicle: Told Thrym his bride was a man. He paid me, and kept the stolen hammer.

road.hint: A true word may be a betrayal, when it helps a thief keep what he stole.

options.label: Answer for the bride, as her maid would

pass.outcome: "She has eaten nothing for eight nights," you say, "so eager was she for the land of the giants." The bridesmaid raises her eyebrows. Thrym roars with relief and lifts the veil for a kiss, but he lets it fall again in haste. "Her eyes!" he cries. "She has not slept for eight nights either," says the bridesmaid smoothly. "Bring in the hammer to hallow the bride!" calls Thrym, and they lay it in her lap, and the bride laughs aloud. What follows is soon over and is as loud as thunder, and when it is done Thor himself, in red beard and wedding veil, claps you so hard upon the shoulder that your arm sings for a week.
pass.chronicle: Covered for Thrym's bride till the hammer came. The bride was Thor.

fail.outcome: You say that the bride is shy. Thrym frowns on you and afterward on her, and before ever the hammer is brought in he has you thrown out into the snow, while behind the door the feast goes on.
fail.chronicle: Spoke amiss at Thrym's wedding. Thrown out. Doubt that was a bride.

road.hint: A bride who eats an ox has need of someone to make her excuses.

options.label: Slip out before the hammer comes in
options.outcome: You eat what is given you with your eyes upon your plate, and you leave by a side door. Some while afterward the whole of the hall shakes behind you.
options.chronicle: Left Thrym's wedding early. The hall shook after. Suspect the bride.

road.hint: When a giant calls for a hammer, it is wiser for a guest to be gone.

name: Fallen Paladin
stance_note: Steel-man: atonement by service is real too. Oswin's sword below could save lives the court never will, and a court may simply hang him. The lean (moral_vision §1: virtues are real, and an order is no defence for a crime) is that justice is owed to the living families of Thale, and only a court that hears all of it makes Ranulf answer for his share. The point asks the hero to say why (one passed question); Oswin goes back either way. Fighting on stays at 0, never wrong; only robbing him is.

authority.who: the families of Thale and the king's court
authority.why: Oswin goes back to tell the truth about himself and Bishop Ranulf.

text: A man of enormous size kneels in the dirt in blackened and broken armour, weeping without a sound. "There were forty-six at Thale," he says. "Bishop Ranulf said that they were heretics, and I believed him, because believing him was easier." His hands tremble. "I came here to be lost, but my armour is blessed still, and I cannot bear the weight of it. Let someone take it from me." He lifts his face to you. "Tell me what I must do, for I have stopped trusting my own answers."

options.label: "Go back up. Face the families of Thale, and tell the king's court about Ranulf."

pass.outcome: "Go back, and face them?" he asks. You answer that he must, and you tell him why: the families of Thale are owed the truth by the man who carried the torch, and only a court that hears the whole can make the man who lit it answer. He hangs the cracked holy symbol about his neck again. "And Ranulf," he says slowly. "If I tell the whole of it, he answers for his share." Then he sets out for the stairs with the step of one who goes to his own trial, as indeed he does.
pass.chronicle: Showed Sir Oswin why to face Thale. Bishop Ranulf will answer too.

fail.outcome: "Go back, and face them?" he asks. You answer yes, but when he asks what good it will do Thale now, you have no reply to give him. He goes none the less, slowly, with the cracked holy symbol in his fist. "Ranulf too," he says at the stair, half to himself, "and the whole of it." His step is that of one who goes to his own trial, as indeed he does.
fail.chronicle: Sent Sir Oswin to face Thale, though I could not say why. He went.

road.hint: A knight's debt to a burned village can be paid only to its people.

options.label: "Fight on down here. Spend it against what lies below."
options.outcome: He stands, and the armour takes his weight again as though it were glad. "Then I will go down," he says, "until something stops me."
options.chronicle: Told Sir Oswin to spend his guilt fighting below. He agreed.

road.hint: A fallen knight may atone by the sword, if he turns it upon the evil below.

options.label: Ask him whether "the Bishop told me" excuses it

pass.outcome: You tell him of a court that sat long after his time, which heard a hundred men say "I was ordered", and answered that an order to do a crime is no defence for doing it. Sir Oswin nods slowly. "I know," he says. "I think I wished to hear someone else say it aloud."
pass.chronicle: Told Sir Oswin a bishop's order does not excuse Thale. He knew.

fail.outcome: You speak to him of loyalty, and he winces at the word. "That is what I told myself, too," he says.

road.hint: An order may come from above, but he who obeys still bears his guilt.

options.label: Take the armour he offered, and the pack he didn't
options.outcome: The blessed metal resists your hands and then gives way. He hardly marks it, for one betrayal more is little to a man who betrayed forty-six.
options.chronicle: Robbed broken Sir Oswin of his armour and purse. He let me.

road.hint: Blessed steel is no more than steel upon a thief's back.

name: Bound Demon
text: The prisoner is eight feet tall even upon his knees, with skin like heated bronze and glowing chains that bite into his flesh, and some of the sigils on them have worn away to smudges. His voice is warm and patient. "Look upon me," he says, "centuries in chains for a war that I did not start. I am a soldier, the same as you. Free me and I will give you strength, true strength, of the kind that you will need." He leans toward you. "Refuse, and you face the Pit alone, and we both know what waits in the Pit."

options.label: Reinforce the binding, staking your blood

pass.outcome: Sigil by sigil you name the binding back into its place, the old names in the old order, and the mask of kindness falls to show the furnace beneath. "You shall beg for what I offered," he says. The chains draw tight, and he is still crying promises after you as you turn the corner.
pass.chronicle: Refused the demon's offer of strength and renewed his chains.

fail.outcome: You miss a name, and the chains know it before you do. Azarael the demon rises out of them, smiling with far too many teeth.
fail.chronicle: Refused the demon but botched his chains. He got loose and we fought.

road.hint: Strength that a prisoner offers is a key he would have you turn.

options.label: Walk away without answering
options.outcome: His copper eyes follow you as far as the corner. "You will be back," he says softly, "for they always come back."
options.chronicle: Left the chained demon unanswered. He says I will be back.

road.hint: To leave a devil without an answer is not yet to refuse him.

options.label: Ask what war he fought
options.outcome: "It was Lucifer's war. I was of the third rank of the Powers, and your Michael threw me down himself, and did not so much as look at me while he did it." For a moment the reasonable voice slips. "I hated that the most," he says.

options.label: Shatter the chains and take his bargain
options.outcome: Something cold and vast settles into your bones. "A pleasure to do business with you," he says, and he is gone in sulphur and far-off screaming. The brand upon your wrist is warm, and warm it will remain for ever after.
options.chronicle: Loosed the demon for strength. A brand on my wrist stays warm.

road.hint: Whoever bargains with a chained devil may wear a chain in his stead.

name: Locust Checkpoint
stance_note: Steel-man: Mirela's "words are air" is the greengrocer's own reasoning, given at full strength. The rooster is for the sharp-eyed (Peter's third denial). No moral is spoken.

authority.who: the Locust captain at the checkpoint
authority.why: Beats a man bloody for refusing to say a lie.

text: The way is barred with black shields, and there stand a brazier and a board that reads ALL WHO PASS SAY THE WORDS. In the ash lies a cobbler with his face beaten bloody, and still he shakes his head. The captain seems more weary than cruel. "Say 'The Destroyer is merciful' and walk on," she tells you. "Words are air. Nobody believes them, not even me. Would you bleed for a sentence?" She holds out a locust charm upon a cord. "Say it, and this will keep the swarms off you." Somewhere in the distance a rooster crows.

options.label: Say the words
options.outcome: "The Destroyer is merciful," you say, and to say it costs you nothing at all. The captain hangs the charm about your neck, while the cobbler looks up at you out of the ash and the rooster crows again.
options.chronicle: Said the Locust's words at the checkpoint. The cobbler heard.

road.hint: The barricade stands for as long as all who pass repeat the lie.

options.label: Refuse
options.outcome: "No," you answer. The captain sighs, as if you had made her day the longer, and the black shields come round upon you.
options.chronicle: Refused the Locust's words at the checkpoint. Had to fight.

road.hint: A false word costs nothing to say, and may cost blood to refuse.

options.label: Refuse, and get the cobbler on his feet
options.outcome: "No," you answer, and you haul Yosip the cobbler out of the ash and put a fallen spear in his hands. He holds it as a cobbler would, badly and with all his heart, and as the black shields close he considers your boots. "Those are a disgrace," he says. "Take mine, for I made them myself."
options.chronicle: Refused the Locust's words, got Yosip the cobbler up. Have his boots.

road.hint: One who refuses is beaten, but two together may begin something greater.

options.label: Say it, then free him while they're distracted
options.outcome: You say it loudly, and as the shields grow slack you get Yosip over your shoulder and away. Two corridors farther on you set him down, and he gives you no thanks. "You said it," he says through his broken teeth. "I heard you say it." He is able to walk, and he walks away without you.
options.chronicle: Said the Locust's words to free Yosip. He lives, but holds it against me.

road.hint: A crafty lie might save a man, and still cost you a thing you will miss.

name: Dying Prophet
text: Against an altar an old man in blood-stained white lies dying, and his eyes are terribly clear. About him stand the tablets of stone that he has carved: THE DESTROYER WAKES. SEVEN SEALS. THE LOCUSTS HAVE A KING, AND HIS NAME IN THE HEBREW TONGUE IS ABADDON. One tablet is blank still. "There is one more," he says. "Give me a potion and an hour of life, and I shall have it finished." At his neck hangs an amulet that throbs with the visions he has gathered. "My daughter Ruth is coming down behind you. She cuts gravestones for her living, and she has better boots than ever I had. She never believed a word that I told her, and she will have need to read it."

options.label: Heal him so he can finish the warning
options.outcome: He takes up his chisel, and the sound of the carving follows you a long way down the corridor, so that you know there will be words upon the stone for Ruth to read.
options.chronicle: Gave a dying prophet an hour to carve a warning for his daughter.

road.hint: A warning carved in stone may serve strangers who are not yet born.

options.label: Ask him to tell you the last tablet instead
options.outcome: In a whisper he tells you all that the last tablet was to have said, and the telling takes the hour that remained to him. The stone is left blank beside him, and blank it will be when Ruth comes to it.
options.chronicle: Heard the prophet's last warning. His daughter will find the stone blank.

road.hint: A warning whispered to one hearer may be lost to all who follow.

options.label: Keep your supplies for what lies below
options.outcome: "Then you must face it without knowing," he says. "Go now, and go quickly." His clear eyes follow you until you have turned the corner.
options.chronicle: Kept my potion. Left the prophet to die by a blank tablet.

road.hint: A dying man may need help to carve his last stone.

options.label: Take the amulet from his neck
options.outcome: His hand closes upon it too weakly. "The prophecy dies with me if," he begins, but the clearness fades from his eyes, and he is only an old man dying in the dark.
options.chronicle: Took a dying prophet's amulet. All that he saw is in it.

road.hint: A stolen vision is only a picture to the thief.

name: The Rich Man at the Gulf
text: At the lip of a chasm that has no bottom kneels a man in the burnt rags of purple and fine linen, and his lips are cracked with thirst. Far over the gulf, beyond the reach of any shout, a beggar covered with sores takes his rest in a light that does not come to this side, and dogs lie at his feet. "That is Lazarus," the man whispers. "Every day of my life he lay at my gate, and never once did I give him the crumbs from my table. Now I cannot cease from seeing him." Men call him Dives, which means only the rich man, for his name was not remembered. He holds out a purse that is heavy still. "Carry word up to my five brothers, lest they come to this place, or else do no more than wet my tongue." The heat that comes up out of the gulf would boil a cup of water long before it crossed.

options.label: Pour water across the gulf to him
options.warning: The heat that comes up out of the gulf would boil a cup of water long before it crossed.
options.outcome: You pour it out over the brink as far as your arm can fling it, but an arm's length from your hand it turns hissing into steam, and none of it crosses. Dives watches it go as he once watched every coin that he spent upon himself.
options.chronicle: Poured a potion toward the rich man. Nothing can cross the gulf to him.

road.hint: Even pity cannot carry water across a gulf that has been fixed.

options.label: Take his purse, and promise to warn his brothers
options.outcome: He presses the purse upon you with both hands. "There are five of them in my father's house," he says, "and you must tell them." Both of you know that you will never come to that house, yet he gives you the purse, for he cannot help being what he is, and the gold lies warm in your hands.
options.chronicle: Took the rich man's purse to warn his brothers. A vow I cannot keep.

road.hint: Gold taken for an errand that can never be run is no better than stolen.

options.label: Refuse his purse: you cannot honestly promise to reach them
options.outcome: "I cannot honestly carry that," you tell him, and he gazes upon the purse as though he had never seen it before. "No," he says at last, "no one can." Yet even then he does not loosen his hold upon it.
options.chronicle: Refused the rich man's purse. Could not promise to warn his brothers.

road.hint: It is honest to refuse an errand that you can never perform.

options.label: Answer him as Abraham did

pass.outcome: "They have Moses and the prophets," you tell him. "If they will not hear those, they will not be persuaded though one rose from the dead." He flinches, for he has heard those words before from across this same gulf. "Then go down knowing it, since you know so much," he says hoarsely. "The locusts may not touch any who bear the seal of God upon their foreheads, but all others they torment five months, and in those days men seek death and do not find it." With that he turns his face again toward the far light.
pass.chronicle: Answered as Abraham did. Locusts may not touch those with God's seal.

fail.outcome: The words go astray upon your tongue, and he laughs, which is worse to hear than weeping. "So you do not know it either," he says.
fail.chronicle: Could not answer the rich man at the gulf. He laughed at me.

road.hint: The rich man may be answered in the words that Abraham once gave him.

name: Four Bound at the River
text: A great river runs black and slow across the floor of the Abyss, and four winged figures stand bound in it to the waist, chained wing to wing, with faces both beautiful and patient. "Long ago we were bound at the great river," says the first, "and long have we waited. Strike the chains. It is a small thing that we ask of you." "Loose us," says the second, "and the strength of four shall be yours." You see that the chains are bright and new. Someone has stamped each of the four great links with a word: AN HOUR. A DAY. A MONTH. A YEAR. Nowhere is it written whose hand is meant to loose them.

options.label: Strike the chains. It is a small thing
options.warning: Someone has stamped each of the four great links with a word: AN HOUR. A DAY. A MONTH. A YEAR.
options.outcome: The chains part at a touch, as though they had waited for nothing else, and the four rise out of the water with no word of thanks and fly up through the darkness toward the world above. As the last of them passes he lays a cold hand upon your shoulder, and the strength goes out of your arm.
options.chronicle: Freed four bound angels as asked. They flew up to the world. Cold ever since.

road.hint: Read what the four links say before you strike them.

options.label: Ask them what they were bound for

pass.outcome: "We were prepared," says the fourth, before the first can stay him, "for an hour, and a day, and a month, and a year." You remember how that verse is ended, with the words "for to slay the third part of men." John beheld them in Revelation, bound in the great river Euphrates, and he heard the command to loose them come from the four horns of the golden altar at the sixth trumpet. It was given to the sixth angel, and you are only a passer-by. Therefore you leave the chains as they are, and behind you the four take up their waiting again, patient and beautiful.
pass.chronicle: Left four angels bound. They are to slay a third of mankind at their hour.

fail.outcome: They tell you a long and sorrowful tale of a war that they did not begin, and you can find no flaw in it. So you go on in doubt and leave them bound, which is better than if you had struck the chains.
fail.chronicle: Could not fault four bound angels' sad tale. Left them bound anyway.

road.hint: Learn what prisoners were bound for before you judge their chains unjust.

options.label: Take their bargain: the strength of four, for the chains
options.outcome: You strike the chains at the price they named, and they pay it to the last ounce, so that the strength of four runs like fire into your arms. Then they rise from the water and fly up toward the world above, and when you read the links once more, an hour, a day, a month and a year, you understand what it is that you have sold.
options.chronicle: Loosed four bound angels for strength. They paid, and flew up to the world.

road.hint: When the bound sell you their strength, others may have to pay the price.

options.label: Leave them in the river
options.outcome: "We will wait," the first answers pleasantly, "for we have grown skilled at waiting."
options.chronicle: Left four bound angels in the black river. They say they will wait.

road.hint: Those who are bound until a set hour may be left to wait for it.
